body:
A debt ratio shows how much debt stands against an economy. It does not show when that debt must be financed again. That distinction matters as euro-area debt reached 88.8% of gross domestic product at the end of June 2026. Vulnerability depends on growth, deficits and refinancing as well as the headline level.

Eurostat published the observation on 21 October. Within the same revised vintage, the March ratio was 88.4% and the year-earlier ratio 87.3%. These figures use a fixed group of 21 euro-area members. The wider EU of 27 countries stood at 82.9% in June; the two geographical groups must not be interchanged.

The same stock can reach the budget at different speeds

A government with large near-term maturities feels a higher new borrowing rate sooner than one whose loans remain fixed for longer. Today’s market yield is therefore not the average interest rate on the entire outstanding stock. The maturity calendar helps determine how quickly financing costs reach public spending.

This can make a quiet interval deceptive: older cheap loans continue while replacement finance is already more expensive. The opposite mistake is to apply one new market yield immediately to all debt. The European interest-cost comparison shows annual expenditure, which answers a different question from a daily bond yield.

France and Greece are more than positions in a ranking

The Greek debt ratio was 140.8% in June and the French ratio 119.1%. Greece stood higher, but its ratio fell from 152.0% a year earlier. France’s rose from 115.4% to 119.1% over the same period.

That does not automatically establish French unsustainability or Greek safety. It shows why level and direction must be read separately. A very high ratio can improve; a lower one can deteriorate. These annual movements use the October data vintage throughout, rather than joining different publication versions.

The separate European debt-ratio ranking gives the broader country order. This analysis asks the next question: how does the stock pass through financing conditions into the budget?

The economy beneath the percentage changes too

The ratio divides gross debt by nominal GDP over the preceding four quarters. That is economic output in money terms, including price changes. If output grows faster than debt, the ratio can fall without any debt repayment. A falling ratio is therefore not the same thing as a budget surplus.

The reverse matters too. Weaker output growth can worsen the ratio even when borrowing grows less quickly than before. A growth forecast remains a forecast: a new quarterly debt release does not automatically update every earlier projection.

Inflation is not a free escape. It can reduce the relative weight of old fixed amounts while also affecting spending and new financing costs. The inflation explorer compares price developments; those observations alone cannot establish debt sustainability.

The budget determines what is added

A government must replace maturing debt and finance any new deficits. Cash management and financial transactions explain why the deficit need not equal the change in debt. Over a longer horizon, spending, revenue and interest costs still need a workable path.

The European fiscal framework combines the 60% debt reference value with national multiyear expenditure paths. Rules do not replace economic assessment. Optimistic growth assumptions can make a plan fragile; poorly designed cuts can weaken its economic base. Implementation and the value created by spending matter as well.

A useful assessment therefore connects measured debt, financing dates and the budget that adds obligations. The debt-to-GDP comparison is a starting point. Those additional facts explain why a similar percentage can represent different problems in different countries.
